Then per connection Username (Active Directory authentication only), CommonName, ClientIp, ConnectionEstablishedTime, ConnectionEndTime, Status and any PostureComplianceStatuses — active connections plus only those terminated within the last 60 minutes. Finally the EC2 instances AWS Config evaluated NON_COMPLIANT because a publicIp field is present in their configuration item.
items.govcloud: Both access paths exist in AWS GovCloud (US-East) and (US-West). Client VPN endpoints there operate using FIPS 140-3 validated cryptographic modules and a fixed cipher set — TLS 1.3 TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 and TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256; TLS 1.2 TLS-ECDHE-RSA/ECDSA-WITH-AES-256-GCM-SHA384 and the AES-128-GCM-SHA256 variants; data channel AES-256-GCM — and AWS advises using the exported client configuration file unmodified rather than configuring other ciphers, which makes AC-17(2) there largely a matter of not breaking the default. Systems Manager runs in both Regions; Change Manager and Incident Manager do not, and State Manager association history cannot be viewed, none of which this recipe touches. ec2-instance-no-public-ip is documented for all supported AWS Regions. Calls to these services must use SSL (HTTPS), and ARNs use partition arn:aws-us-gov
items.notes: The commands split cleanly across the control family, and the gap in the middle is the one to be honest about. AC-17(1) — automated monitoring and control of remote access — is what session history and connection logs deliver, with two documented blind spots. Session Manager does not log sessions that connect through port forwarding or SSH, because SSH encrypts the session data inside the TLS connection and Session Manager is only the tunnel; an operator who port-forwards leaves a session record with no command content behind it. And describe-sessions reaches back 30 days only, so anything longer is an S3 or CloudWatch Logs query against the destinations named in the preferences document, not an SSM call. Client VPN retention is shorter still — terminated connections drop out of the API after 60 minutes, which makes the log group named in ConnectionLogOptions the only durable record, and Username is populated only for Active Directory authentication, so certificate-authenticated users are identified by CommonName or not at all. AC-17(2) is the strongest link in GovCloud, where the endpoints are FIPS 140-3 modules by construction; the Session Manager equivalent is kmsKeyId in the preferences document, and it is empty unless you set it, so an empty kmsKeyId is a finding rather than a default. AC-17(3) — routing remote access through managed network access control points — is the one nothing here proves. Session Manager and a Client VPN endpoint are managed access points, and ec2-instance-no-public-ip is the closest negative check, but that rule applies only to IPv4 and only to AWS::EC2::Instance: an IPv6-reachable instance, a load balancer fronting SSH, or a third-party jump host is invisible to it. Read the result as 'no EC2 instance carries a public IPv4 address', which is a useful sentence and not the control. AC-17 itself — the documented usage restrictions, configuration requirements and per-type authorization — is a record you write, and this telemetry only shows whether the estate matches it. One warning to carry into the evidence package: Session Manager logs the commands entered and their output, so a credential typed into a session lands in the log group you are about to hand an assessor.

items.evidence: A demonstration run against the live log estate that audit records can be reduced, sorted and searched on demand by event criteria — the standing saved queries, the query that ran, and the report it returned

commands.name: logs-insights-start-query
commands.run: aws logs start-query --log-group-names <LOG_GROUP_NAME> --start-time <START_EPOCH> --end-time <END_EPOCH> --query-string 'fields @timestamp, userIdentity.arn, eventName, sourceIPAddress | filter eventName = "ConsoleLogin" | sort @timestamp desc | limit 1000'

commands.name: lake-start-query
commands.run: aws cloudtrail start-query --query-statement "SELECT eventTime, eventName, userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress FROM <EVENT_DATA_STORE_ID> WHERE eventName = 'ConsoleLogin' ORDER BY eventTime DESC LIMIT 1000" --delivery-s3-uri s3://<EVIDENCE_BUCKET>

commands.name: start-query-execution
commands.run: aws athena start-query-execution --work-group primary --query-execution-context Database=cloudtrail_logs --result-configuration OutputLocation=s3://audit-reports-bucket/athena/ --query-string "SELECT eventtime, useridentity.arn, eventname, sourceipaddress FROM cloudtrail_logs WHERE eventname = 'ConsoleLogin' ORDER BY eventtime DESC LIMIT 1000"

items.expected_output: First the saved CloudWatch Logs Insights query definitions — queryDefinitionId, name, queryLanguage of CWLI, SQL or PPL, the queryString itself and the log groups each is scoped to — which is the standing reduction-and-reporting capability as configured rather than as claimed. Then a queryId, and against it the matching records: at most 100,000 log events per query and 10,000 returned per get-query-results call, one query spanning at most 50 log groups, a 60-minute runtime ceiling and a Region-wide limit of 100 concurrent Insights queries. Then the event data stores with Status (CREATED, ENABLED, PENDING_DELETION, STARTING_INGESTION, STOPPING_INGESTION or STOPPED_INGESTION), RetentionPeriod in days from 7 to 3,653, MultiRegionEnabled, OrganizationEnabled and TerminationProtectionEnabled. Then a QueryId from CloudTrail Lake whose results are delivered to the S3 URI you named, and a QueryExecutionId from Athena whose results land in the workgroup's OutputLocation. Keep the query text beside its output — the pair is the evidence and neither half is evidence alone.
items.govcloud: All three query paths run in both AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. Athena's only documented difference is that granting AWS Lake Formation permissions to Athena users who authenticate through the JDBC or ODBC driver with a SAML identity provider is unavailable. CloudWatch Logs is available with Live Tail missing and the logGroupNamePattern parameter unsupported on DescribeLogGroups — neither affects an Insights query. CloudTrail Lake is available, but Lake integrations, query generation, query results summarization, event data stores for AWS Config configuration items, AWS Audit Manager evidence and events from outside AWS, and the Activity summary widget are not: you write the SQL yourself, and non-AWS audit records cannot be pulled into the same store for reduction. One scoping trap: since 22 November 2021 CloudFront, IAM and AWS STS events are recorded in AWS GovCloud (US-West), so a single-Region search from US-East silently misses every global-service event unless the trail is multi-Region. Calls must use SSL (HTTPS) and ARNs use partition arn:aws-us-gov
items.notes: AU-7 asks for a capability, so the honest evidence is a query that ran rather than a configuration that exists — run one and keep the query text beside its output. AU-7(1), processing and sorting records by event criteria, is exactly what the filter and sort clauses in the Insights query and the WHERE and ORDER BY in the Lake and Athena statements demonstrate; pick criteria an assessor cares about — a named principal, a source IP, an event name, a bounded window — rather than a bare SELECT *. The half of AU-7 that no output proves is the requirement that reduction not alter the original content or time ordering of the records: these are read APIs, and Athena queries the CloudTrail objects in place in S3 rather than rewriting them, but that is an argument from the API contract, not a line in the result set — the property is actually carried by log file validation and object immutability, which belong to the integrity recipe, not this one. Two limits deserve to be read before the query power is. A query can only reduce records that reached the log group or the event data store, so a 90-day retention makes an annual report impossible no matter how good the SQL, which is why the retention fields are pulled alongside. And the Insights ceilings — 100,000 events per query, 10,000 per page, 50 log groups, 60 minutes — mean a broad search across a year of CloudTrail truncates silently rather than failing, so a result set sitting exactly at the limit is a truncated report and must not be filed as a complete one; Athena and CloudTrail Lake have no such row ceiling and are the right tools for a long look-back. Whether the resulting report actually supports after-the-fact investigation is a human judgement about the query, which is what keeps this partial rather than full.

items.evidence: Audit records read back and checked for content, rather than a setting that implies records exist. AU-03 asks what is IN a record — the type of event, when and where it occurred, its source, its outcome and the identity behind it. This recipe pulls the most recent management events out of CloudTrail and asserts that the fields carrying type, time and location are populated on the records that actually came back. It also lists the trails and the CloudWatch log groups, so the record sources this recipe does not read appear in the same output as the one it does.
items.expected_output: From record-sample, Events[]: one page of at most fifty of the most recent management events in the calling Region. Passing --max-results turns off the CLI's automatic pagination, so this is a sample and never the ninety-day window. Each row is the projection CloudTrail returns for a lookup: AccessKeyId, CloudTrailEvent, EventId, EventName, EventSource, EventTime, ReadOnly, Resources[] of ResourceType and ResourceName, and Username. All nine members are documented Required: No. That is the most important fact about this output, and it is why every clause below filters the rows rather than projecting a field. EventSource is the service the request was made TO. CloudTrailEvent is a JSON STRING holding the whole record body — eventVersion (1.11 at time of writing), userIdentity, eventTime, eventSource, eventName, awsRegion, sourceIPAddress, userAgent, errorCode, errorMessage, requestParameters, responseElements, requestID, eventID, eventType, eventCategory and the rest. It is not a parsed object, so no field path can reach anything inside it. The eventContext enrichment is never present in lookup-events output. The rows come from event history. AWS describes event history as a record of the past ninety days of management events in a Region, and states it is separate from any trails or event data stores. From trails, trailList[] with Name, S3BucketName, IncludeGlobalServiceEvents, IsMultiRegionTrail, HomeRegion, TrailARN and LogFileValidationEnabled, and S3KeyPrefix, SnsTopicARN, CloudWatchLogsLogGroupArn, CloudWatchLogsRoleArn, KmsKeyId, HasCustomEventSelectors, HasInsightSelectors, IsOrganizationTrail and RecursiveLogging where configured. Shadow trails — the copies of a multi-Region trail in other Regions — are returned by default. From log-groups, logGroups[] with logGroupName, creationTime, retentionInDays, metricFilterCount, arn, storedBytes, kmsKeyId, dataProtectionStatus, inheritedProperties, logGroupClass, logGroupArn and the other members the reference lists, in pages of at most fifty.

assertions.description: The lookup returned at least one record, so the content clauses below run over a real population rather than an empty one. An empty page means the calling Region had no management events in the last ninety days. It does NOT mean no trail exists: AWS states that event history is separate from any trails, so this clause and every clause below pass on an account that has never created one.

Every record returned identifies the type of event, AU-03's first limb. Written as a filter that selects records where EventName is missing, because the member is documented Required: No. A projection over Events[].EventName would drop exactly those records and pass.
Every record returned says when the event occurred, AU-03's second limb. Same offender form, for the same reason: EventTime is Required: No, so the rows to catch are the ones missing it.

Every record returned names the service the request was made to, which is AU-03's where limb. It is not the source limb. The source of the event — the calling address and client, sourceIPAddress and userAgent — exists only inside CloudTrailEvent, and a human reads it there.

Every record returned carries the full record body. This clause proves the body arrived and deliberately claims nothing about its contents. CloudTrailEvent is a JSON string, so the source, the outcome and most of the identity inside it cannot be reached by a field path. The clause marks the line between what this recipe decides and what a human reads.

items.govcloud: AWS CloudTrail and Amazon CloudWatch Logs are both available in AWS GovCloud (US-West) and AWS GovCloud (US-East). Every ARN in this output uses partition arn:aws-us-gov. Three partition differences bear on what a record contains. First, CloudTrail enriched events are not supported in AWS GovCloud (US), so eventContext is absent from records in this partition; it is also absent from lookup-events output everywhere. Second, network activity events exist here only for AWS KMS, Amazon S3, AWS CloudTrail and AWS Secrets Manager, so the AwsVpceEvents eventType covers fewer sources than the commercial documentation describes. Third, since 22 November 2021, global service events from CloudFront, IAM and AWS STS are recorded in the Region where they were created, which is AWS GovCloud (US-West). A single-Region trail in AWS GovCloud (US-East) does not receive them, and AWS directs such trails to become multi-Region. That cuts against this recipe. Event history and lookup-events show those events in the Region where they occurred, so the sample can return an IAM event that no trail in the calling Region captured. The sample proves what records contain; it does not prove that a trail captured them. If you use Direct Connect, AWS directs you to enable CloudTrail in the standard AWS account rather than the AWS GovCloud (US) account. On export control: AWS states that CloudTrail logs do not contain export-controlled data and that CloudTrail configuration data may not contain it. For CloudWatch Logs, AWS lists log group names, log stream names and log group tags among the data that may leave the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and describe-log-groups returns the first and third, so neither should name anything export-controlled. The logGroupNamePattern parameter of describe-log-groups is not available in the partition; this recipe does not use it.
items.notes:
AU-03 names six things a record must identify: the type of event, when it occurred, where it occurred, its source, its outcome, and the identity of the subject. CloudTrail's record schema carries all six. This grammar can decide three of them from fields: type from EventName, when from EventTime, and where from EventSource, the service the request was made to. Identity is partly visible in the top-level Username, but it is not asserted, because events AWS services make on their own have no human requester. The source (sourceIPAddress, userAgent) and the outcome (errorCode, responseElements) are only inside CloudTrailEvent, which is a JSON string, so a human reads them there.

The rating is partial for three reasons. Parsing that string would fix only the last of them. (1) AU-03 covers every audit record in the system, and CloudTrail records only AWS API activity. Application logs, operating-system logs and anything the reader's own software writes have whatever content their author chose, and no clause here reads them. describe-log-groups and describe-trails are collected so those other sources are listed beside the one that was read. (2) The population is a sample of at most fifty recent events, not the record stream, so a clean result says those records were well-formed. (3) Source and outcome sit inside a string the grammar cannot address.

The record clauses do NOT depend on a trail, and this is the easiest thing to misread. AWS states that CloudTrail is enabled by default, and that event history is separate from any trails or event data stores. An account that has never created a trail still returns a full Events[], and every content clause below goes green. Those clauses therefore say nothing about whether records are being kept past ninety days, centralized, or protected from change. Those are AU-11, AU-12 and AU-09, and config-cloudtrail-audit-logging and audit-log-retention-and-delivery-failure claim them. This recipe collects describe-trails as inventory and deliberately asserts nothing over it: a trail clause here would re-prove a neighbouring control under AU-03's name.

The same fact bounds the indicator claim. KSI-MLA-OSM asks for a SIEM or similar system giving centralized, tamper-resistant logging, and FedRAMP maps AU-03 to it. This recipe serves that indicator only through record content. Event history is a single account's per-Region view, not a centralized one, even though AWS calls it immutable. Centralization and tamper resistance are proved, where they are proved at all, by the trail recipes.

Every member of the Event type is documented Required: No, EventId, EventName, EventTime and EventSource included. So each clause is a filter that selects the rows missing a field, asserted count_eq 0, and never a projection of the field across rows. A projection would drop the rows where the member is absent and report success over the rest. What the clauses assert — that the records this account actually returned carry the field — is a stronger claim than anything AWS promises.

The population clause fails only on an empty page, and an empty page means the calling Region had no management events in the last ninety days. It never means there is no trail. Read it that way before anything else.

items.evidence: Checks whether the continuous monitoring the reader believes is running has actually run. The question is about the programme, not one named rule. Is the recorder recording? Does any Config rule in the account fail to produce a current result? Are the standards and scanners that make up the rest of the programme in a state that yields findings? The clauses are built around one answer that looks like success and is not: a rule that has never been evaluated reports neither compliant nor non-compliant.
items.expected_output: From configuration-recorders, ConfigurationRecorders[] with name, roleARN, arn, and a recordingGroup of allSupported, includeGlobalResourceTypes, resourceTypes, exclusionByResourceTypes and recordingStrategy. Each also has a recordingMode whose recordingFrequency is CONTINUOUS or DAILY, and service-linked recorders carry servicePrincipal. allSupported true means Config records every supported type and picks up new types as AWS adds them. allSupported false means it records only the enumerated list, and a newly supported type is NOT recorded until somebody adds it. From configuration-recorder-status, ConfigurationRecordersStatus[] with name, recording, lastStartTime, lastStopTime, lastErrorCode, lastErrorMessage, lastStatusChangeTime, arn, and a lastStatus of Pending, Success, Failure or NotApplicable. Those lastStatus values are mixed case, unlike the upper-case enums elsewhere in this output. From config-rules, ConfigRules[] with ConfigRuleName, ConfigRuleArn, ConfigRuleId, Description, Scope, InputParameters, CreatedBy and EvaluationModes. Source.Owner is AWS, CUSTOM_LAMBDA or CUSTOM_POLICY. The optional MaximumExecutionFrequency is One_Hour, Three_Hours, Six_Hours, Twelve_Hours or TwentyFour_Hours, and a periodic rule runs every twenty-four hours by default. ConfigRuleState is ACTIVE, DELETING, DELETING_RESULTS or EVALUATING. From config-rule-evaluation-status, ConfigRulesEvaluationStatus[] with ConfigRuleName, ConfigRuleArn and ConfigRuleId, plus the invocation, evaluation, activation and error timestamps and FirstEvaluationStarted. AWS documents FirstEvaluationStarted false as meaning Config has not finished evaluating your resources against the rule at least once. Called with no rule names, the call returns status for all Config managed rules you use; the reference does not say whether custom rules are included. From config-rule-compliance, ComplianceByConfigRules[] with ConfigRuleName and a Compliance of ComplianceType plus ComplianceContributorCount (CappedCount, CapExceeded). ComplianceType is COMPLIANT, NON_COMPLIANT or INSUFFICIENT_DATA for this data type. INSUFFICIENT_DATA means no current evaluation results are available, for one of three reasons: the rule has never been invoked, its function is not delivering results, or every result was NOT_APPLICABLE because the resources were deleted or removed from the rule's scope. From security-standards, StandardsSubscriptions[] with StandardsSubscriptionArn, StandardsArn, StandardsInput, StandardsStatusReason, StandardsControlsUpdatable (READY_FOR_UPDATES or NOT_READY_FOR_UPDATES), and a StandardsStatus of PENDING, READY, INCOMPLETE, DELETING or FAILED. From guardduty-detectors, DetectorIds[]. From guardduty-detector, a Status of ENABLED or DISABLED, a FindingPublishingFrequency of FIFTEEN_MINUTES, ONE_HOUR or SIX_HOURS, ServiceRole, CreatedAt, UpdatedAt, Tags, Features, and DataSources. The API reference marks DataSources deprecated, so read Features. From inspector-status, accounts[] with accountId, a state of status, errorCode and errorMessage, and a resourceState carrying ec2, ecr, lambda, lambdaCode and codeRepository, each with its own status. Status values are ENABLING, ENABLED, DISABLING, DISABLED, SUSPENDING and SUSPENDED. Accounts the call could not answer for go to failedAccounts[] instead of accounts[].

assertions.description: The configuration recorder is on. This is the population clause for everything Config-based below: rules cannot evaluate resources whose configuration is not recorded, so a FAIL here makes the rule clauses meaningless, not merely red. An account with no recorder returns an empty list, and this clause comes back UNPROVEN.

No recorder's most recent recording event failed. Asserted against Failure rather than for Success because a recorder that has just started legitimately reports Pending, and demanding Success would fail a healthy estate. The value is mixed case as documented.

At least one Config rule is active. This is the population clause for the two evaluation clauses below, which are count_eq 0 and would otherwise pass on an account with no rules. The pipe matters: without it, [0] indexes each matched object instead of the filtered list.

Every rule the evaluation-status call returns has completed at least one evaluation. AWS documents FirstEvaluationStarted false as meaning Config has not finished evaluating your resources against the rule at least once. Comparing against the JSON literal true catches false rows and rows where the field is missing. Called with no names, the call is documented to return all Config managed rules you use, so the claim covers managed rules. Whether custom rules appear is not stated.

No rule reports that no current evaluation results are available. Without this clause, 'no rule is NON_COMPLIANT' is true on an estate where nothing has run, because AWS returns INSUFFICIENT_DATA, not NON_COMPLIANT, in that case. AWS documents three causes: the rule was never invoked, its function is not delivering results, or every result was NOT_APPLICABLE because the resources were deleted or removed from its scope. The third can occur on a healthy estate. A FAIL is a prompt for a human to decide which cause applies, not a finding in itself.

At least one Security Hub standard is subscribed. This is the population clause for the status clause below, and the only evidence in this recipe that the estate is measured against a published benchmark rather than only against rules somebody chose.

Every subscribed standard finished enabling. PENDING means Security Hub is still adding controls, and INCOMPLETE means it could not enable the standard completely. Both describe a standard that is attached and not fully measuring. READY means Security Hub runs checks for every applicable enabled control, but it describes the subscription, not results. AWS documents up to twenty-four hours to generate or update control findings, and up to twenty-four hours for a preliminary score in AWS GovCloud (US).

The detector the reader named is enabled. A detector can exist in a DISABLED state, and list-detectors still returns its id while nothing is analysed, which is why this clause reads the status rather than the id. It serves CA-07's monitoring breadth and deliberately not KSI-MLA-EVC, because GuardDuty evaluates behaviour, not configuration.

The Inspector status call returned at least one account. This is the population clause for the state clause below, which is count_eq 0 and would otherwise pass on an empty accounts[]. That happens when the call answers for nobody, because accounts it cannot answer for go to failedAccounts[] instead.

No account came back in failedAccounts[]. An account Inspector could not answer for is missing from accounts[], not present and failing, so the state clause cannot see it. Written as not_exists on the first entry, so the clause passes whether an empty failedAccounts is returned as [] or omitted.

No account in accounts[] has an Inspector state other than ENABLED. The documented values include ENABLING and SUSPENDING, which are transitional, and DISABLED and SUSPENDED, which are not. All four fail here; re-run before acting on the transitional two. This reads the account-level state only. resourceState carries a separate status for each scan type, and a human should read it before treating a PASS as coverage of EC2 or ECR.

items.govcloud: All four services run in AWS GovCloud (US-West) and AWS GovCloud (US-East). The differences that matter here are about what the programme can cover, not whether it exists. AWS Config publishes a separate managed-rule availability list for each of the two GovCloud Regions, so a rule set built commercially will not deploy whole in the partition, and the shortfall differs between US-East and US-West. Config cannot record third-party resources or custom resource types in the partition, so allSupported means everything Config supports HERE, and SSM documents for Config remediation actions are unavailable. Security Hub CSPM does not support every control in AWS GovCloud (US), publishes its own per-Region list of unsupported controls, lacks some integrations, and aggregates across Regions only between the two GovCloud Regions. AWS states that in the China Regions and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, "it can take up to 24 hours for Security Hub CSPM to generate a preliminary security score for a standard". Separately, control findings can take up to twenty-four hours to generate or update. So a standard enabled this morning in the partition can read READY and have evaluated nothing. Amazon Inspector in AWS GovCloud (US) has neither Lambda Code Scanning nor Managed Code Repository Scanning, so resourceState.lambdaCode and resourceState.codeRepository cannot reach ENABLED there. The account-level clause below reads only state.status and is unaffected. Amazon GuardDuty in the partition lacks the entity-lists capability (IP address lists remain), lacks the IAM finding type CredentialAccess:IAMUser/CompromisedCredentials, and lacks a named set of EKS audit-log AnomalousBehavior finding types. An ENABLED detector there therefore watches for fewer things than a commercial one. AWS Config metadata must not contain export-controlled data, and AWS names rule-evaluation annotations among the fields that must not carry it.
items.notes:
CA-07 has two halves, and this recipe reads one of them. The operating half is telemetry: is the recorder on, do the rules evaluate, which standards are enabled, do the scanners cover the account. The clauses below decide that half. The half the control actually names is a strategy: which metrics were chosen, how often they are checked, who correlates the results and who reports them. No call returns that document, and the telemetry is what the document is measured against, not a substitute for it. Hence partial.

The vacuity this recipe closes is not the usual empty list. describe-compliance-by-config-rule returns INSUFFICIENT_DATA, not NON_COMPLIANT, for a rule that has never run. So the obvious clause, "no rule is NON_COMPLIANT", is TRUE on an estate where no rule has ever been evaluated. Two clauses below close the gap. One asserts FirstEvaluationStarted is true on every rule the evaluation-status call returns, which catches a rule that has never completed an evaluation. The other asserts no rule reports INSUFFICIENT_DATA, which also catches a rule that has stopped producing results. That second clause fails in one healthy case: a rule whose resources were all deleted or moved out of its scope. A FAIL there needs a human to decide which of AWS's three documented causes applies, and the clause is kept anyway, because without it the compliance output passes on an idle estate.

Other recipes here assert FirstEvaluationStarted for the rules they name. This one is unfiltered, so it claims something about the whole set the call returns. That set is documented as all Config managed rules you use. The reference does not say whether CUSTOM_LAMBDA and CUSTOM_POLICY rules are included, so the claim is made for managed rules. A custom rule absent from the response is outside the clause, not proved live.

recordingGroup.allSupported is collected but deliberately not asserted. A recorder with allSupported false and an explicit resourceTypes list is a legitimate design, not a defect, and turning it into a FAIL would be an architectural judgement this site has no standing to make. What deserves a human's attention is the consequence AWS documents: with allSupported false, a newly supported resource type is not recorded until somebody adds it, so the recording group ages. Read exclusionByResourceTypes beside it.

The indicator claim needs one qualification stated plainly. KSI-MLA-EVC asks that the configuration of machine-based information resources — "especially infrastructure as code" — be persistently evaluated and tested. This recipe evaluates DEPLOYED configuration only. Nothing here reads a template, a plan or a policy-as-code result before deployment, and that half of the indicator belongs to the pipeline plane. The Config and Security Hub clauses serve the indicator. The GuardDuty and Inspector clauses name only ca-7: GuardDuty evaluates behaviour and Inspector evaluates software vulnerabilities, and neither reads configuration. They are here because CA-07's monitoring programme is broader than its configuration half.

StandardsStatus READY means Security Hub can run checks and calculate a score. It does not mean it has. AWS documents up to twenty-four hours to generate or update control findings, and up to twenty-four hours for the preliminary score in AWS GovCloud (US). On the Config side, the INSUFFICIENT_DATA clause catches an enabled programme with no evaluations. Security Hub has no equivalent clause here, and this recipe does not pretend otherwise.

lastStatus is asserted against Failure, not for Success, on purpose. The documented values are Pending, Success, Failure and NotApplicable, and a recorder that has just started legitimately reports Pending. A clause demanding Success would fail a healthy estate. Failure is the only value that is unambiguously wrong.

Inspector's account-level state is what the clause reads. resourceState carries a separate status for each scan type, and the reference does not say whether an account can be ENABLED while its EC2 or ECR scanning is not. A human should read resourceState before treating an account-level PASS as coverage of a particular resource type.

Every call here is Regional. A programme that is complete in one Region and absent in another returns a clean result from whichever Region you called. That is the largest gap between what this recipe proves and what CA-07 asks.

items.evidence: For each artifact actually running in the boundary, the cryptographic answer to whether it came from the build this provider claims built it: the signed provenance statement, the certificate identifying the workflow that produced it, and the countersigned timestamps that make the signature checkable later — which for this recipe's predicate type on a public repository are transparency-log entries, are not that for every attestation the same digest carries, and are not that at all for a private repository — the normal case inside a boundary — where GitHub's own Sigstore instance keeps no transparency log; a distinction the notes draw because it decides who can re-check the evidence. Collected alongside the two things that decide whether that answer can be trusted at all — the version of the verifying client, and the record of which deployed artifacts were submitted for verification in the first place.

commands.name: verify-results
commands.run: gh attestation verify oci://<REGISTRY>/<IMAGE>@<DIGEST> --repo <ORG>/<REPO> --predicate-type https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1 --format json

items.expected_output:
Report names used below, and the command each comes from: `gh-version` is the first command, `ecr-repositories` the second, `deployed-images` the third, `verify-results` the fourth, `attestations` the fifth, `attestation-bundles` the sixth and `trusted-root` the seventh. The third report name reads `deployed-images` for the registry image rows.

THIS RECIPE IS TWO NESTED LOOPS AND BOTH ARE LOAD-BEARING. Run the third command ONCE PER REPOSITORY NAME returned by the second — `describe-images` takes a single `--repository-name` and there is no organization-wide form of it — and run the fourth and fifth ONCE PER DIGEST returned by the third. Walking one repository and reading its images as the registry's is the same arithmetic error the sibling recipes on this plane call out by name, and here it lands on the command that IS the scope claim, so it under-states the population rather than merely under-reporting a setting.

From `gh --version`, the client version string. It is collected rather than decorative — see the CVE paragraph in the notes.

From the registry calls, the repository names in the account and, per repository, one row per image with its `digest`, `pushedAt` and `tags`. This is the widest population the commands can establish, it comes from the estate rather than from the platform under assessment, and `scan_scope` says what it is still not.

From the verify call with `--format json`, GitHub documents "a JSON array containing one entry per verified attestation", each entry carrying an `attestation` (the verified bundle) and a `verificationResult` whose parsed contents include `signature.certificate` — the parsed X.509 certificate identifying the signer — `verifiedTimestamps`, an array of transparency-log and timestamp-authority records, and `statement`, carrying `subject`, `predicateType` and the `predicate` object. The command's documented purpose is to "Verify the integrity and provenance of an artifact using its associated cryptographically signed attestations", validating "the identity of the actor that produced the attestation" and "the expected attestation predicate type (the nature of the claim)". `--predicate-type` defaults to `https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1` and is written out explicitly in the command above rather than left implicit, for the reason the notes give. Other flags worth knowing exist rather than being used blind: `--cert-identity` and `--cert-identity-regex`, `--cert-oidc-issuer` (default `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`), `--signer-repo`, `--signer-workflow`, `--source-ref`, `--source-digest`, `--deny-self-hosted-runners`, `--digest-alg` (default `sha256`), `--limit` (default 30), `--bundle` and `--custom-trusted-root`.

From the attestations REST call, a JSON OBJECT — not an array, and it is the only command in this file whose stdout is not one. THE BODY IS THINNER THAN AN EARLIER DRAFT OF THIS PARAGRAPH CLAIMED, and the difference is why an assertion over it was first rewritten and then deleted altogether. Each entry in the `attestations` array carries `repository_id`, `bundle_url`, `initiator` and a `bundle` key — and on the live endpoint `bundle` is NULL. The signed material is not inline: it is served from `bundle_url`, a time-limited signed blob URL carrying its own expiry in the query string, and the object behind that URL is the Sigstore bundle proper (`mediaType` `application/vnd.dev.sigstore.bundle.v0.3+json`, `verificationMaterial`, `dsseEnvelope`), served compressed rather than as plain JSON. The earlier draft described that inner object as though the GET returned it, which is the POST request body's shape rather than the GET response's; the rendered REST reference documents only `repository_id`, `bundle_url` and `initiator` for the 200, and a live call confirms the fourth key is present and null. `gh attestation download <ARTIFACT> --repo <ORG>/<REPO>` is the supported route to the bundle itself and writes a `.jsonl` named for the digest; a `bundle_url` copied into a report expires and is not an archival reference. The path parameter is documented as `sha256:HEX_DIGEST`, `predicate_type` filters to "provenance, sbom, release, or freeform text for custom predicate types", `per_page` maxes at 100 and defaults to 30, and a fine-grained token needs `attestations:read`. One reassurance worth stating on a plane where the opposite is usually true: this endpoint DOES filter on its path parameter — the same call against an all-zero digest returned `{"attestations":[]}` — so an empty array here means the platform holds nothing for that digest rather than that the question went unasked. A `bundle_url` present for a digest is therefore a real and useful thing to report — the platform holds material an assessor can go and fetch — and it is reported here rather than asserted as a clause, because retrievability of a blob is not a statement about whether the artifact was modified. The notes record why a clause over it was written and then deleted.

From the download call, a `.jsonl` written to the working directory and named for the subject digest — GitHub documents that it downloads "attestations associated with an artifact for offline use" and that "Any associated bundle(s) will be written to a file in the current directory named after the artifact's digest", with a dash replacing the colon on Windows. It is in this recipe for two reasons. It is the only command here that yields a copy of the signed material that KEEPS, which the expiring `bundle_url` does not; and an authoring run found it succeeds on an artifact for which `gh attestation verify` reports "no attestations found", so running both is how an assessment distinguishes "nothing is attested" from "this invocation would not accept what is". It takes the same `--predicate-type` filter and was run WITHOUT it to establish that.

The seventh command writes the trusted root out for an air-gapped assessment: GitHub documents that "Artifact attestations can be verified without an internet connection" given the bundle, the trusted root file and the CLI imported in advance, and advises generating "a new `trusted_root.jsonl` file any time you are importing new signed material into your offline environment".

assertions.description: The verification returned at least one attestation whose parsed statement can be read. This clause exists because of CVE-2025-25204: on affected GitHub CLI versions the command exited ZERO when no attestation matched the requested predicate type, so the absent case looked like the passing case to anything reading `$?`. What the failure looks like on a PATCHED client was measured during authoring and is not an empty array: stdout is zero bytes and the message goes to stderr. The shape an AFFECTED client produces was not measured — no client in the v2.49.0–v2.66.x range was run — so whether this clause reports RED or an unparseable document on that path is undetermined and is stated rather than assumed. Either way it does not report success, which is the property the exit status lacked — and that is checked against the engine rather than asserted: an absent or unreadable output evaluates to `unproven`, and an empty array reaches this clause as a null — `[0]` of `[]` — which `exists` evaluates to a fail. Neither is a pass, and the second is a clean red rather than an abstention. Written against the parsed JSON rather than the exit status for that reason, and paired with the collected `gh --version` so an assessment can say which client produced the answer. It speaks for one digest — the population is the two nested loops in `expected_output`, not this clause. For SR-10 this is the inspection itself rather than a precondition for one: a readable statement is the artifact having been examined and a verdict returned. What it is not is the schedule — the clause says an inspection happened, never that it happens at the frequency SR-10 asks the organization to define.

items.notes:
SI-07 (07) asks the provider to incorporate the detection of organization-defined security-relevant unauthorized changes INTO THE ORGANIZATIONAL INCIDENT RESPONSE CAPABILITY. The detection half of that sentence is the strongest thing this plane has: verification of a signed provenance statement over a named artifact is cryptography, not inference, and it either checks out or it does not. The other half is not in this output anywhere. Nothing here shows that a verification failure raises an incident, that an incident is triaged, that it reaches a human, or that a deployment is stopped. The gap is the integration and not the detection, and the disposition this recipe spends said so in advance precisely so that the authoring batch would not read the strength of the command as covering the clause it does not touch. It does not.

SR-10 IS THE SECOND CONTROL THIS RECIPE CLAIMS, AND IT IS THE ONE THE COMMAND FITS BEST. SR-10 asks the provider to inspect an organization-defined set of systems or components — at random, on a defined frequency, or upon indication of need — to detect tampering. Verifying a signed provenance statement is that inspection performed on the software share of that set: it is pointed at one artifact, it returns a verdict about whether that artifact is what the recorded build produced, and the verdict is cryptographic rather than inferred. Where SI-07 (07) reads this output and finds the detection half strong and the incident-response half missing, SR-10 reads the same output and finds the inspection ACT present and three other things absent. Same rating, different reason, and the reasons are worth separating because a reader who has satisfied one has not satisfied the other.

What SR-10 asks for that this output does not hold. The DESIGNATED SET is the first: SR-10's object is organization-defined, and nothing in a verification result says which artifacts the organization designated. `scan_scope` above is this recipe's answer to that and it is a reconciliation performed outside the command, not a field in its output. The FREQUENCY is the second, and it is the same gap that keeps the rating off `full` for SI-07 (07): the verification event leaves no timestamp anywhere in this output, so "at random or [frequency]" cannot be evidenced from it at all. The HARDWARE share is the third and it is not this plane's to close — SR-10's object is systems OR COMPONENTS, the physical ones are inspected by AWS under the shared responsibility model, and the AWS verdict on this control says exactly that and rates `narrative` for it. The two verdicts are deliberately different words and the register holds both. A reader who takes this recipe as SR-10 coverage has taken the software limb of a control whose object is wider, and the control page says so because the verdicts are per plane.

Why SR-10 is claimed here rather than in a second recipe. The collection is the same, the scope claim is the same reconciliation, and the AWS plane's settled convention is one recipe per collection claiming every control that collection's output speaks to — `config-cloudtrail-audit-logging` claims AU-02, AU-09 and AU-12 from one CloudTrail read. A second recipe would have duplicated `scan_scope` verbatim, and `scan_scope` is this plane's hardest field and the one where two copies drifting apart would do the most damage. This is the pipeline plane's first multi-control recipe; the cost of the choice is that the notes now have to say which paragraph argues which control, which is what the headings do.

KSI-SVC-VRI is added alongside KSI-MLA-EVC and it is the better fit of the two. VRI asks the provider to "use cryptographic methods to validate the integrity of machine-based information resources", which is a one-sentence description of what this recipe does; EVC, chosen when the recipe covered only SI-07 (07), is argued below as the least-bad of three and that argument still stands for the control it was chosen for. Both are connected claims in the crosswalk's own terms — EVC reaches SI-07 (07), VRI reaches SR-10 — which is the property `overlay-ksi-crosswalk.test.ts` holds this plane at zero violations of. SVC-ACM and SVC-EIS also reach SR-10 and are NOT claimed: ACM is about configuration managed by automation and reviewed for drift, and a provenance verdict is neither a configuration nor a drift review; EIS is about persistently evaluating resources for opportunities to improve security, which this output does not do.

A LIVE RUN ON 2026-09-12 PRODUCED THREE FACTS THAT CHANGED THIS RECIPE, recorded with their commands because two of them contradict what an earlier pass wrote from the documentation alone.

First, the REST body. `gh api /repos/cli/cli/attestations/sha256:<DIGEST>` returned one entry whose keys were `repository_id`, `bundle_url`, `initiator` and `bundle`, with `bundle` set to NULL. The assertion this recipe used to carry asserted that `bundle.dsseEnvelope` existed, so it would have gone RED on a healthy estate — the inverse of this plane's usual failure and no better, because a check that cannot pass gets switched off by the first person who runs it. The replacement clause it got asserted `bundle_url`, which is the key the response actually carries; that clause is written up below too, with why it was deleted in its turn. What the live call changed for certain is the PROSE: `bundle_url` is how an assessor reaches the signed material, and `expected_output` says so. The same call against an all-zero digest returned `{"attestations":[]}`, so the endpoint does filter on its path parameter.

Second, the transparency log, and this is the fact an earlier draft of this paragraph over-read — twice, in both of the ways this recipe exists to warn about. The bundle behind that `bundle_url` had NO `verificationMaterial.tlogEntries` KEY AT ALL, with `timestampVerificationData.rfc3161Timestamps` in its place and a signing certificate issued by `O=GitHub, Inc.`, `CN=Fulcio Intermediate l1`. The draft called that "an EMPTY array", which is exactly the absent-is-not-false error the paragraphs below delete an assertion over, committed in the prose describing them. It then generalised the finding to public repositories at large, and that was wrong in the direction that misleads a reader about their own builds. The same release's `gh_2.100.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz` carries TWO attestations for one digest: GitHub's release attestation, `initiator` "github", the one described above; and the Actions build provenance, `initiator` "user", predicate type `https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1`, signed through `O=sigstore.dev` / `CN=sigstore-intermediate`, WITH a `tlogEntries` array of one. Verifying that second one returns `verifiedTimestamps` of `[{"type": "Tlog", "uri": "https://rekor.sigstore.dev", ...}]`. So on a public repository this recipe's own predicate type does land in the Public Good Instance's transparency log, as the cited concept page says; the no-transparency-log property belongs to the private-repository path and to GitHub's own attester, and a reader who took the draft's sentence at face value would have believed something false about their own estate. The narrower finding still stands and is still worth the paragraph: ONE DIGEST CAN CARRY ATTESTATIONS WITH DIFFERENT TRUST ROOTS, and which one an invocation gets depends on the `--predicate-type` it asked for.

Third, and the one an implementer should read before budgeting for this recipe: THE VERIFY COMMAND RETURNED "no attestations found" FOR AN ARTIFACT THAT IS ATTESTED. `gh attestation download gh_2.100.0_checksums.txt --repo cli/cli` wrote the bundle successfully. `gh attestation verify gh_2.100.0_checksums.txt --repo cli/cli` on the same file with the same client (v2.97.0, well past the CVE fix) exited 1 with `Error: no attestations found` — with the default `--predicate-type`, with the predicate type the stored attestation actually carries (`https://in-toto.io/attestation/release/v0.2`, which is a release attestation and not SLSA provenance), and with `--no-public-good`. Passing the downloaded bundle in explicitly with `--bundle` takes TWO invocations to read and an earlier draft reported them as one. `--bundle` alone fails with `Error: no attestations found with predicate type: https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1` — which names the world it is in, unlike the fetch path. `--bundle` together with `--predicate-type https://in-toto.io/attestation/release/v0.2` fails with `Error: verifying with issuer "GitHub, Inc."`, a trust-root outcome rather than an absence. So the fetch path inside `verify` applies a filter that `download` does not, and the word it prints for the result is "found". A provider whose report is built from verify output will see one sentence cover "this artifact was tampered with", "this artifact was never attested", "this attestation is of a kind this invocation will not accept" and "this client does not trust the issuer that signed it". That is the plane card's vacuity trap wearing a non-empty error message, and it is the strongest argument in this file for why both ratings are `partial` and why `scan_scope`'s reconciliation against an inventory held outside the platform is load-bearing rather than ceremonial. The four-worlds collapse is a property of the FETCH path — the command as this recipe runs it. The `--bundle` path separates two of the four by naming the predicate type and the issuer in its error, which is a concrete improvement available to an implementer and the reason `attestation-bundles` is now collected: download first, then verify against the downloaded bundle, and "never attested" stops looking like "attested with something this invocation will not take". This recipe does not yet write that two-step into a clause, and a later batch should. It is also the CVE's trigger condition observed in the wild on a patched client: an attestation that exists with a predicate type other than the one asked for is exactly the case CVE-2025-25204 reported as exit zero, and here a fixed client exited 1 as it should.

The field path the clause below reads is OBSERVED, not merely documented. An earlier draft of this paragraph said the opposite — that no successful verification could be produced during authoring — and that was an artefact of having drawn every live fact from `gh_2.100.0_checksums.txt`, which is the one file in that release carrying no build provenance at all. Against `gh_2.100.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz` in the same release, `gh attestation verify <FILE> --repo cli/cli --predicate-type https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1 --format json` exits 0 and returns a one-element array whose `verificationResult` carries `mediaType`, `signature`, `verifiedTimestamps`, `verifiedIdentity` and `statement`, with `statement.predicateType` equal to the predicate type asked for. `verifiedIdentity` is not named in the manual's prose and is where `--cert-identity` and `--signer-workflow` would be checked. An implementer should still expect to spend the first hour of this recipe on those flags and the trusted-root ones rather than on parsing.

THE EXIT STATUS IS NOT THE EVIDENCE, AND THERE IS A CVE THAT PROVES IT. The obvious way to write this recipe is to run the command in CI and trust its exit code — which is what makes CVE-2025-25204 the single most important fact in this file. GitHub's own advisory for the GitHub CLI states that `gh attestation verify` "may return an incorrect zero exit status when no matching attestations are found for the specified `--predicate-type <value>`", that this happens when "an artifact has an attestation with a predicate type different from the one provided in the command", that the cause was "a re-used uninitialized error variable" returning `nil` "when no matching attestations are found", and that "Users who rely exclusively on the exit status code of `gh attestation verify` may incorrectly verify an attestation when the attestation's predicate type does not match the specified predicate type in the command". Versions from v2.49.0 are affected; v2.67.0 is the fix. Read what that says about this plane, because it is the plane card's vacuity trap arriving in the one place the card said `full` was plausible: the ABSENCE of a matching attestation was reported as success. The clause below is therefore written against the PARSED JSON rather than against the exit code, `--predicate-type` is written out explicitly in the command rather than relied on as a default, and `gh --version` is collected so that an assessment can state which client produced the result. A recipe on this plane that reduces to `run the command, check $?` is unsound on a client older than v2.67.0 and is unverifiable on any client whose version was never recorded.

THREE ASSERTIONS HAVE NOW BEEN WRITTEN, AUDITED AND DELETED FROM THIS RECIPE. All three are recorded here so that a later batch reading the thin assertion list does not helpfully restore them. The first two went before the recipe shipped; the third went in the batch that added SR-10, and it is the one a reader is most likely to think was fine.

The first asserted `verify-results[?verificationResult.verifiedTimestamps==null] count_eq 0` — that no returned attestation lacked the transparency-log records that make its signature checkable later. It was unfalsifiable, and the way it failed is the exact shape this plane's card warns about. Verification requires at least one observer timestamp to succeed, so an attestation with none never appears in the output at all: it is ABSENT from the response, not false in it, and the clause therefore returned zero on every possible output of the command, including on an estate where nothing verifies. The literal was wrong twice over besides — a bare `null` is not a JMESPath literal in the form this file uses elsewhere, and the field is an empty array rather than null in any case — but the fatal defect is the one no rewrite of the expression could repair. It read as the recipe's most confident clause and decided nothing. That it appeared in the one recipe whose whole argument is that this plane must not trust a signal reporting success on absence is the reason it is written up here at length rather than quietly dropped.

The second asserted `verify-results[?verificationResult.statement.predicateType!='https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1'] count_eq 0` — that every returned entry carried the predicate type asked for. It cannot fail either, for a duller reason: the command is invoked WITH `--predicate-type https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1`, so on a patched client the returned set is already filtered to it, and on an affected client the array is empty and the surviving existence clause is what catches that. A clause restating the flag it was invoked with is an invariant, not a check. What it was really trying to say belongs where it now is — in the command, written out explicitly rather than left to a default.

The third was `attestations.attestations | [0].bundle_url` `exists`, and it is this batch's own. It replaced a clause asserting `bundle.dsseEnvelope` — which was simply wrong, since the GET returns `bundle` as null, and which therefore could not pass on any estate — and the replacement was true, could go red, and was not vacuous: the all-zero digest returns `{"attestations":[]}` and `[0].bundle_url` does not exist on it. It was deleted anyway, for the reason that matters more than whether a clause works: IT DID NOT DECIDE EITHER CONTROL. `bundle_url` says the platform holds a retrievable blob for the digest. It does not say the artifact is unmodified, which is what SI-07 (07) reads this output for, and it does not say an inspection returned a verdict, which is what SR-10 reads it for. It is green for an attestation of any predicate type from any initiator, including one the verifying client then refuses on trust-root grounds. The proof that it was measuring a different thing is on this recipe's own counterexample: for `gh_2.100.0_checksums.txt` the `bundle_url` clause is GREEN while the verification clause has no document to read at all, so the two clauses disagreed about the single artifact these notes hold up as the failure case, and the weaker one passed. A retrievability statement is a real thing to want and belongs in `expected_output`, which now carries it, rather than in a clause that lights a control page.

What remains is one clause, which is fewer than this recipe started with and fewer than it had an hour ago. That is the honest count: of everything these seven commands return, exactly one field decides anything about either control, and the paragraphs above are why each of the others does not.

Why this is `partial` and not `full`, stated against the schema's own two tests rather than by assertion. The writable check exists — the clause below is it. The freshness clause does not: a `full` rating on this plane additionally needs a `max_age_days` assertion showing the scan RAN, RECENTLY, over a named set, and there is nothing in this output to hang one on. `verifiedTimestamps` carries transparency-log and timestamp-authority records, but those timestamp the SIGNING of the attestation, not the running of the verification, and a freshness clause over them would assert that the artifact was built recently — a different claim, and one that is false for a correctly pinned long-lived dependency. The verification event itself leaves no timestamp in this output at all. So the honest reading is that the population cannot be shown to have been re-verified on any cadence from the evidence the recipe collects, which is the second reason the rating is `partial` and the reason it would remain `partial` even if the incident-response limb were somehow answered.

What an attestation proves, in GitHub's own words, and what it does not. The concept page states that "Artifact attestations enable you to create unfalsifiable provenance and integrity guarantees for the software you build" and that "Artifact attestations by itself provides SLSA v1.0 Build Level 2". It also carries the sentence that belongs in every assessment reading this evidence: "It is important to remember that artifact attestations are *not* a guarantee that an artifact is secure. Instead, artifact attestations link you to the source code and the build instructions that produced them." A verified artifact is an artifact whose origin is known. SI-07 (07) is about unauthorized CHANGE, and provenance answers that limb well; it says nothing about whether the authorized build was itself sound, which is SA-11's and SI-07's own territory.

The signer identity is where this recipe is weakest as written, and it is deliberate. The command validates "the identity of the actor that produced the attestation", but the clause below does not pin WHICH actor: `--cert-identity`, `--cert-identity-regex`, `--signer-repo`, `--signer-workflow` and `--source-ref` are the flags that would, and the right values for them are provider-specific — the workflow file and ref that legitimately builds this artifact. A verification that passes without them says the artifact was built by SOME workflow in the named repository, which is a real claim and a weaker one than most readers will assume. `--deny-self-hosted-runners` is the same shape: a provider whose threat model distinguishes hosted from self-hosted runners has a flag for it and this recipe does not set it. Pinning these is the single highest-value change an implementer can make to this recipe, and it is left to the implementer because a wrong value here fails closed and noisily rather than silently.

The registry commands are AWS calls inside a pipeline recipe, and that is on purpose rather than an oversight about which file this belongs in. `scan_scope` requires an inventory held OUTSIDE the scanner, and a scanner that cannot enumerate anything makes the requirement bite harder here than anywhere else on this plane — so the enumeration has to come from the estate. They are written against ECR because that is the estate this project's other plane describes; a provider deploying Lambda packages, AMIs or plain binaries substitutes the equivalent enumeration and the recipe is unchanged in every other respect. Nothing about the verification is AWS-specific. What these commands are NOT is the control's population, and `scan_scope` now says so at length rather than implying otherwise: a registry listing is what was pushed, the deployment record is what is running, and an earlier draft of that field described the second while enumerating the first.

KSI-MLA-EVC is claimed and the other two indicators reaching this control are not, and the claim is the weakest judgement in this recipe rather than a settled one. EVC asks that the configuration of machine-based information resources, especially infrastructure as code, is persistently evaluated and tested. Two of its words strain here. `Persistently` is the one the missing freshness clause fails to evidence, and it is named elsewhere in these notes. `Configuration` is the harder one and is recorded rather than argued away: an artifact's provenance is not its configuration, EVC's other controls are `ca-7`, `cm-2` and `cm-6` — configuration-baseline controls, which is the company the indicator keeps — and the honest statement is that verifying what a deployment was built from is a test applied to a machine-based information resource before it becomes one, which is adjacent to the indicator's subject rather than inside it. EVC is claimed because it is the least-bad of the three indicators that reach this control and because the evidence is real; a batch that later finds a better home for this recipe should move it without treating this paragraph as a defence. KSI-MLA-LET asks for a maintained and reviewed list of information resources and event types that will be logged, monitored and audited; a verification result is not that list. KSI-MLA-OSM asks for a SIEM or similar system used for centralized, tamper-resistant logging; the Sigstore transparency log is genuinely tamper-resistant logging, but it is the signing infrastructure's log rather than the provider's monitoring system, and claiming OSM from it would be reading someone else's control as evidence of yours. Both omissions are the same judgement the incident-response gap makes: the route from this output into the provider's own response and monitoring capability is exactly what is missing, and claiming the indicators that describe that route would be claiming it.

items.evidence: Patch Manager compliance state plus Amazon Inspector scan status and coverage — proving flaws are being found continuously (Inspector enabled and actually covering your resources) and that the fixes landed (per-node missing/failed patch counts and the time of the last scan or install)
items.expected_output: An EvaluationResults array with an empty NON_COMPLIANT set (every SSM patch-compliance record reads COMPLIANT), InstancePatchStates showing MissingCount/FailedCount/CriticalNonCompliantCount/SecurityNonCompliantCount at zero with a recent OperationEndTime, an account status whose resourceState.ec2/ecr/lambda read ENABLED, and coveredResources whose scanStatus.statusCode is ACTIVE with a recent lastScannedAt. Managed rule identifier: EC2_MANAGEDINSTANCE_PATCH_COMPLIANCE_STATUS_CHECK
items.govcloud: AWS Config, Systems Manager, and Amazon Inspector are available in AWS GovCloud (US-East) and (US-West); instance and finding ARNs use partition arn:aws-us-gov. Two GovCloud differences to record: Lambda code scanning is not available, and the Inspector plugin for Linux deep inspection is not FIPS compliant.
items.notes: This proves flaws are detected and shows exactly what is still missing and when patching last ran — it does not prove the remediation clock was met. Whether an open finding sits inside your SI-02 timeframe, or carries an approved deviation or POA&M entry, is a judgement joined against your risk-acceptance record, not an API result. Substitute your real instance ids and account id; describe-instance-patch-states requires --instance-ids (use describe-instance-patch-states-for-patch-group to sweep a patch group). Note also that patch compliance data is a point-in-time snapshot and each successful scan overwrites the previous one, so capture the output at collection time rather than reconstructing history later.

items.evidence: Cryptographic proof that the audit trail CloudTrail delivered has not been altered or deleted, plus the compliance state of the write-once controls that make stored records and container images tamper-evident

commands.name: config-rule-evaluation-status
commands.run: aws configservice describe-config-rule-evaluation-status --config-rule-names cloud-trail-log-file-validation-enabled s3-bucket-default-lock-enabled ecr-private-tag-immutability-enabled

items.expected_output: Three EvaluationResults arrays, a validation run and a vault description. Empty NON_COMPLIANT sets mean every trail signs digest files, every evaluated bucket has Object Lock on by default and every private ECR repository refuses to move a tag. validate-logs prints the window it actually found and two ratios — for example '3/3 digest files valid' and '15/15 log files valid'; any shortfall names the file. describe-backup-vault returns Locked true with a LockDate, the UTC instant the compliance-mode grace time ends. Managed rule identifiers: CLOUD_TRAIL_LOG_FILE_VALIDATION_ENABLED, S3_BUCKET_DEFAULT_LOCK_ENABLED, ECR_PRIVATE_TAG_IMMUTABILITY_ENABLED Then the configuration recorder status, whose recording flag must be true, and one ConfigRulesEvaluationStatus row per rule named, with FirstEvaluationStarted true and a LastSuccessfulEvaluationTime — the two facts that make an empty NON_COMPLIANT set mean something.

assertions.description: Every trail has log file validation on.
Every evaluated bucket has Object Lock enabled by default.
Every private ECR repository has tag immutability on.
Vault Lock is currently protecting the named vault — AWS defines true as delete or update operations on its recovery points failing.

The customer-managed configuration recorder is on — with no recorder the list is empty and this is UNPROVEN, and with a stopped one an empty NON_COMPLIANT set is indistinguishable from a clean estate.

Every one of cloud-trail-log-file-validation-enabled, s3-bucket-default-lock-enabled, ecr-private-tag-immutability-enabled has evaluated at least once; a deployed-but-never-evaluated rule also returns an empty result, and a rule that is not deployed makes the call fail rather than return nothing.
Each rule has a successful evaluation on record.

items.govcloud: All five calls work in AWS GovCloud (US): none of the three managed rules names a GovCloud Region in its exclusion list, and AWS Backup Vault Lock is documented among the features offered for all supported resources with no Region carve-out — unlike restore testing and logically air-gapped vaults, which are blank for both GovCloud rows in the feature-availability table. Trail, bucket, vault and repository ARNs use partition arn:aws-us-gov, and because CloudTrail uses a different key pair per Region, validate the logs in the Region that produced them
items.notes: The strong claim here is narrow and worth stating precisely. validate-logs is real cryptography — SHA-256 hashing with SHA-256/RSA signing, an hourly digest file that references the last hour's log files and carries the signature of the previous digest — so a clean run positively asserts that the delivered log files were not modified or deleted, and can even assert that no log files were delivered in a window you believed was empty. What it will not do: validate files you moved, since they must stay where CloudTrail put them; and it cannot report tampering across a gap — disable validation for an hour and no digest exists for that hour, so the chain simply breaks. Enabling the feature is not the same as checking it, which is why both the Config rule and the CLI run belong here: the rule proves digests are being produced, the run is the only thing that verifies them. Object Lock and Vault Lock are prevention, not detection — they make a deletion fail rather than proving none happened, and Object Lock only counts if the mode and period match your policy: the rule's optional mode parameter is what pins GOVERNANCE versus COMPLIANCE, and unset it passes either. Vault Lock in governance mode can be removed by anyone holding the IAM permission, so read Locked together with LockDate — before that date even a compliance-mode lock is still removable. The honest gap is the host: SI-7 asks for integrity verification of software, firmware and information, and nothing above watches a filesystem. ECR tag immutability stops a tag being repointed at a different image but says nothing about drift inside a running instance; file integrity monitoring is third-party or self-built on AWS, and SI-7(1)'s ‘defined frequency’ is a policy number you compare against, not an API result. Finally, a NON_COMPLIANT-only query returns an empty array on success and says nothing about resources Config never evaluated — join it against recorder coverage before reading emptiness as compliance.

items.evidence: The machine-generated inventory of every resource an external entity can reach — IAM Access Analyzer's active ExternalAccess findings — read against the declared zone of trust, so the terms-and-conditions review has a list to work from rather than a memory
items.expected_output: From list-analyzers, one row per analyzer with type ACCOUNT or ORGANIZATION for external access (the ACCOUNT_UNUSED_ACCESS, ORGANIZATION_UNUSED_ACCESS, ACCOUNT_INTERNAL_ACCESS and ORGANIZATION_INTERNAL_ACCESS types answer different questions and do not produce ExternalAccess findings) and status one of ACTIVE, CREATING, DISABLED, FAILED. From list-findings-v2, one finding per resource shared outside the zone of trust, each with resource, resourceType, resourceOwnerAccount, findingType, status, createdAt and analyzedAt. From describe-organization, the organization id, FeatureSet ALL or CONSOLIDATED_BILLING, and the management account id — the boundary an ORGANIZATION analyzer treats as internal. From the Config rule, an empty NON_COMPLIANT set means an external-access analyzer is enabled and ACTIVE in that Region.
items.govcloud: IAM Access Analyzer and Organizations operate in GovCloud (US); analyzer and resource ARNs use partition arn:aws-us-gov. The Config managed rule IAM_EXTERNAL_ACCESS_ANALYZER_ENABLED is NOT available in either GovCloud (US) Region — its published availability excludes GovCloud (US-East) and GovCloud (US-West) — so in GovCloud the fourth call has no rule to query and the analyzer's own status field from list-analyzers is the evidence that it is enabled.
items.notes:
AC-20 is a two-limb control and only one limb is in this output. The limb that is here: which external entities can reach organization-controlled information. Access Analyzer answers that by logic-based reasoning over resource-based policies, and every access by a principal INSIDE the zone of trust is trusted by definition, so a finding is exactly an access that crosses the boundary the organization declared. The limb that is not here: whether each of those crossings is covered by terms and conditions consistent with the trust relationship. That is an agreement — a contract, an interconnection security agreement, an authorization to connect — and no call returns it. Attach the agreement register and reconcile it finding by finding; the reconciliation, not the finding list, is the AC-20 artifact.

The inventory also has a direction. Access Analyzer sees resources you share OUT. It does not see an external system your people use to process organization information — a SaaS tool reached from a workstation leaves no resource policy in your account and produces no finding. That half of AC-20 has to come from your own third-party register, and inventing a join between the two would make the coverage claim wider than the evidence.

Three scope facts worth pinning down before the count is quoted. External-access analysis is REGIONAL: an analyzer evaluates only resources in the Region where it is enabled, so one analyzer per Region in use, or the inventory is silently partial. Fifteen resource types are analyzed for external access — S3 buckets and directory buckets, IAM roles, KMS keys, Lambda functions and layers, SQS queues, Secrets Manager secrets, SNS topics, EBS volume snapshots, RDS DB and DB cluster snapshots, ECR repositories, EFS file systems, DynamoDB streams and tables — and a resource type outside that list is not covered by the analyzer at all. And findings refresh within about 30 minutes of a policy change but can lag up to 24 hours when a change notification is missed, so a finding list is a recent state, not a live one.

items.evidence: The advisories AWS itself has issued against this account — operational issues, scheduled changes and account notifications, each dated and scoped — together with the subscribers on the topic those alerts are published to and the confirmation state of each subscription, which is the difference between an address that was entered and an address that receives
items.expected_output: From describe-events, events[] with arn, service, eventTypeCode, an eventTypeCategory of issue, accountNotification, scheduledChange or investigation, region, availabilityZone, startTime, endTime, lastUpdatedTime, a statusCode of open, closed or upcoming, and an eventScopeCode of PUBLIC, ACCOUNT_SPECIFIC or NONE — the field that says whether an advisory is a general service event or one raised against this account in particular. The API is served from a global endpoint, global.health.amazonaws.com, which resolves by CNAME to whichever of the us-east-1 (active) and us-east-2 (passive) endpoints is current, and AWS notes that only the active endpoint carries the latest data. From list-subscriptions-by-topic, Subscriptions[] with SubscriptionArn, Owner, Protocol, Endpoint and TopicArn, up to 100 per call with a NextToken beyond that. Read SubscriptionArn carefully: for a subscription that has not been confirmed it is not an ARN at all but the LITERAL STRING PendingConfirmation, which AWS's own published response for an unconfirmed email subscriber shows. That is the discriminator, and it is on this list. From get-subscription-attributes, an Attributes MAP whose values are all strings — including PendingConfirmation, documented as "true if the subscription hasn't been confirmed", and ConfirmationWasAuthenticated, "true if the subscription confirmation request was authenticated" — which is why any clause on them would compare against the string "false" and not a boolean. This call is collected as supplementary evidence — ConfirmationWasAuthenticated is not derivable from the list — and carries no assertion, because it takes --subscription-arn and the unconfirmed case has no ARN to pass it.

assertions.description: The security alert topic has at least one subscriber. A topic with none is an alerting path that terminates in nothing. Says nothing about WHO the subscribers are — that is a comparison against the personnel your policy names, and no call returns that roster — and on its own it does not even prove deliverability, since an unconfirmed subscription satisfies it too. Read it with the clause below, never alone.

No subscriber on the alert topic is still unconfirmed. AWS returns the literal string PendingConfirmation in the SubscriptionArn column for a subscription nobody has confirmed, so the failing case is a value in the list rather than an absence — which is why this clause reads the list and not the per-subscription attributes, whose call cannot even be made for an unconfirmed subscriber.

items.govcloud: Amazon SNS operates in both AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and topic and subscription ARNs use partition arn:aws-us-gov. The AWS Health call is the one to check before this recipe is planned rather than after, and its constraint is commercial as much as GovCloud: AWS states that a Business, Business+, Enterprise On-Ramp, Enterprise or Unified Operations plan is REQUIRED to use the AWS Health API, and that an account not enrolled in one receives a SubscriptionRequiredException. A provider on Basic or Developer support cannot run the first command at all, and for them the advisory-receipt half of this recipe is a Health Dashboard record — which every customer can see — rather than an API result. In GovCloud the endpoint is different in kind, not just in name: AWS documents the Health API there as a single regional endpoint in us-gov-west-1, as opposed to the commercial global endpoint with failover-capable Regions behind it, so the global.health.amazonaws.com DNS-lookup pattern does not apply and us-gov-west-1 is the target. Two further GovCloud behaviours worth writing into the assessment: some Health events are global rather than Regional — IAM's among them — and receiving those requires a rule in AWS GovCloud (US-West), the twin of the CloudTrail Region rule the PS-04 recipe names; and the EventBridge channel there does not deliver public Service Health View events at all, so an alerting pipeline built on EventBridge sees account-specific events only and the API or the RSS feed is what carries the rest.
items.notes:
SI-05 has four movements: receive security alerts, advisories and directives from external organizations on an ongoing basis; generate internal security alerts; disseminate them to the personnel your policy names; and implement directives or notify the issuing organization of the degree of nonconformance. This output touches the first and the third, and only for one external organization.

That organization is AWS. Health events are the vendor's own notifications to this account — operational issues, scheduled changes, account notifications — dated, scoped by eventScopeCode to this account or to the service generally, and enumerable. That is a real answer to 'are you receiving advisories from your suppliers, on an ongoing basis, and can you show it'. The supply-chain indicator is claimed on one limb of its statement and not the whole: KSI-SCR-MON allows for mechanisms that 'may include contractual notification requirements', and a vendor health feed is exactly such a mechanism. It is NOT the other limb — none of Health's four event categories is a vulnerability category, and this evidence monitors AWS's service health rather than the provider's third-party software inventory.
